C01.why: Mostly server-authoritative state swaps with almost no physics. The hard parts are the volume of content (the pitch says 120+ anomalies) and the CCTV: a live ViewportFrame grid means cloning the world every frame, which is too expensive on mobile, so it has to be camera-CFrame switching. Chase pathfinding and revive are standard.
C01.fix: Launch with about 40 anomalies built from 6 data-driven primitives (swap, move, tint, animate, spawn NPC, sound). Make CCTV a tap grid of static thumbnails that switches the camera to one live feed at a time.

C02.why: The device and rule generator is pure, testable logic, and the role views are just local rendering. The hardest problem is information security: the Book's rules and the Eyes' colours must be sent per player through remotes, not as replicated instances, or exploiters can read them. A mandatory 3-player group also needs party pads or queue infrastructure at low CCU.
C02.fix: Use in-server party pads instead of cross-server matchmaking, and launch with 5 module types instead of a broad procedural set. Ship 2-player Eyes+Book as the primary mode so solo-with-one-friend works on day 1.

C03.why: Classic shared-physics-body problem: only one client can own the raft. It has to be server-owned with input sent over remotes, so every paddler feels 100–300 ms of input lag on mobile. Roblox terrain-water buoyancy is unreliable for custom craft, so buoyancy and current have to be scripted, and every 3–4 min river course is hand-built.
C03.fix: Don't use free physics. Simulate the raft as a custom kinematic controller on a river spline (lateral offset, yaw, speed), stepped on the server and interpolated on clients. Ship 3 courses and 2 vehicle layouts.

C04.why: UI and inspection driven with negligible networking. The hardest problem is the content pipeline: each item needs variants with visible tells (stamps, UV paint, weight). Roblox has no custom shaders, so the UV reveal is done with SurfaceGui/Decal toggles under a masked tool. The forger PvP mode adds hidden-role logic and balancing.
C04.fix: Cut Forger Night from launch and generate tells as layered decals and attribute flags on about 15 base meshes instead of bespoke fake models.

C05.why: Many unanchored props are grabbed, thrown and hidden by 3–6 clients, which means constant network-ownership handoffs, replication load and fling exploits by whoever owns the part. The server also has to track 'evidence' state reliably (under a rug, behind the dog, glued vase) across physics chaos. Every house is a dense, hand-dressed asset set.
C05.fix: One house at launch, at most 40 tagged evidence props with simple hide-zones (no fracture or paint-fluid sim). Make grab server-owned with a short client-side visual lead.

C06.why: Standard tycoon/incremental architecture (plots, grid placement, DataStore, numbers) with plenty of existing patterns. The 'shared pile' is a server number plus a scaled mesh. The hardest problem is the performance of many animated machines across a 20+ player server, plus economy balancing.
C06.fix: Machines are visual-only (no physical conveyed parts; output is computed per tick), with client-side animation LOD and a cap of about 30 machines per plot.

C07.why: Hardest pitfall on the list: a RopeConstraint between characters owned by different clients makes each client's physics fight the others. That produces jitter, rubber-banding and flings, which is why the 2024 Chained Together clones feel bad. It also needs a custom snap-to-ledge climbing controller with climb animations, stamina, anchor-catch logic and a daily procedural mountain.
C07.fix: Drop the physical rope: a server-validated soft leash applied locally to each client's own character (spring toward the partner's replicated position) with a purely visual verlet rope. Ship 2–3 handcrafted peaks instead of daily procedural ones.

C08.why: Ghost AI with several behaviours, procedural room assembly and camera-frustum tagging on the server are all doable. The montage theatre is a CFrame/animation record-and-replay system (store entity transforms at about 10 Hz for tagged windows, then replay on dummy rigs in the lobby), which is fiddly and bug-prone, and the lobby↔mission teleport has to carry data.
C08.fix: Replace the replay montage with static 'thumbnail cards' (one frozen frame per tagged moment, posed rigs plus a caption). Ship one location with 4 ghost types.

C09.why: The $1 gesture recognizer is easy on the client, but it can't be validated on the server: the client's classification has to be trusted under cooldowns and rate limits. Multitouch on mobile (thumbstick plus drawing pad plus camera drag) is a known input-sinking headache. The spell-combo matrix grows N², each combo needs VFX, and wave defence needs lightweight non-Humanoid enemies to stay performant.
C09.fix: 4 elements and 6 hand-authored combos, enemies moved server-side as anchored CFrame entities rendered client-side, and the gesture set limited to 6 very distinct shapes.

C10.why: Low networking risk: a deterministic auto-battle sim on the server, rendered on the client. The hardest problem is design and content: a genetics/mutation system that stays balanced, modular critter rigs where mutations attach as parts while keeping animations valid, and per-player critter storage and versioning in DataStores.
C10.fix: One shared rig family (all critters on one skeleton with swappable parts and palettes) and cosmetic-only mutations plus 3 stat genes at launch. Defer co-op runs and cross-pairing.

C11.why: Liminal art is cheap (simple geometry and lighting). The hardest problem is a noise-driven Entity AI that is fair and scary on procedurally stitched room modules: PathfindingService on generated layouts needs careful module connectors and recomputation. Carry/weight, extraction and the hub are standard.
C11.fix: Hand-built rooms stitched on a fixed grid with pre-placed nav waypoints (custom graph instead of runtime PathfindingService), and a single Entity type at launch.

C12.why: Ownership is manageable because only the pilot drives (give the pilot network ownership of the plane). The hard part is a mobile-friendly arcade flight model with takeoff and landing detection, plus 3 distinct role UIs and an emergency state machine. Each new aircraft is a model, cockpit UI and tuning pass.
C12.fix: Make flight semi-scripted (pilot steers within a corridor along a route spline; landing is an approach mini-game, not free-flight physics) and launch with one aircraft.

C13.why: A 50-player server simulating an OpenFront-style pixel territory grid (tens of thousands of cells with troop flow) needs custom buffer-based delta replication and EditableImage rendering. Parts would kill performance. Server tick cost is high, and filling 50 slots at low CCU requires competent strategy bots. Exploit-proof server authority is mandatory, which makes this very hard for a small team.
C13.fix: Use 12–16 players on a province map (about 150 nodes instead of a pixel grid), with bots to fill and a 10-minute match. Graph-based state replicates trivially.

C14.why: It combines three Roblox physics pitfalls: driving a vehicle with loose parcels inside (fling and jitter in moving frames), two-person carry of one physics object owned by two clients, and impact damage measured from velocity spikes, which turn noisy around ownership transfers. That is plus vehicle feel and several dressed neighbourhoods.
C14.fix: Cut free driving (a short auto-drive or cutscene between stops) and use a scripted 'linked carry' where both carriers' movement is constrained server-side to a carried anchor instead of a shared physics body. Compute damage from scripted collision events, not raw physics.

C15.why: The auto-battle sim and the merge/elimination logic are straightforward server code on a 4×4 board, and toys can be tween-animated rather than rigged. The hardest problems are reliably filling 8-player lobbies at low CCU (bots must draft sensibly), arbitrating the shared conveyor under latency, and the unit/synergy roster plus balance work needed for depth.
C15.fix: Launch with 6-player lobbies auto-filled by heuristic bots and about 20 toys with 4 traits. Draft from per-player shops instead of a contested shared conveyor.

C16.why: Interact-prompt chores, timers and NPC pet state machines with pathfinding are well-trodden. The hardest problem is animation and AI content: each pet species needs a full anim set and believable escape/mischief behaviours, and each home is a dressed level.
C16.fix: 2 pet species (cat, dog) sharing one AI framework and 2 homes at launch, with chaos events as scripted sequences instead of emergent AI.

C17.why: Small scope with few assets. The hardest problem is that tall stacks of irregular unanchored parts in Roblox physics jitter, creep and never fully sleep. They have to be server-owned for one shared truth, and clients see the tower lag-interpolated while they aim placements. Wind and quake events make determinism worse.
C17.fix: Auto-anchor pieces once they have settled below a velocity threshold for 1 s, and unanchor only within an event radius during wind or quakes. Ship co-op only before versus.

C18.why: Roblox servers are ephemeral and players land in random servers, so a monster raised by 'your server' all week is really a persistent cross-server entity. That needs MemoryStore/DataStore UpdateAsync contention handling and a definition of membership (guilds). The Saturday cross-server battle has to be coordinated through MessagingService under its rate limits, or simulated once and broadcast. The infrastructure risk is high relative to the gameplay.
C18.fix: Tie the monster to opt-in clans. Compute the weekly battle once in a scheduled job (one server claims a MemoryStore lock), store the result and play it back as a canned replay in every server.

C19.why: Low physics, and 30 NPC statues are cheap if anchored. The hardest problem is fair, exploit-resistant 'caught moving in the beam' detection. Character movement is client-authored, so the server sees positions about 150 ms late: a player who froze on their own screen can be tagged unfairly, and an exploiter can spoof stillness. That needs grace windows and server-side movement sanity checks.
C19.fix: Make freeze a server-confirmed state (pressing Freeze locks the character server-side and immunity starts on the server's acknowledgment, with a 0.3 s grace window). Launch with one museum and 6 pranks.

C20.why: Tap-to-target makes the ball a deterministic parabola, cheap to replicate (start, target and time) and simulated identically on every client. One court is minimal art. The hardest problem is competitive fairness: hit windows and who touched first under 100–300 ms mobile latency need lag compensation, and ranked needs MMR plus queue infrastructure at low CCU.
C20.fix: Launch casual 2v2 and 3v3 with in-server queue pads and server-authoritative hit windows (no ranked or cross-server matchmaking until CCU supports it).

overall_notes: Biggest separator is physics on shared objects. Anything where several clients influence one physics body (rope between characters C07, two-person carry plus vehicle cargo C14, shared raft C03) or many grabbable props (C05) carries Roblox network-ownership jitter, fling and exploit risk, and it is far cheaper if faked with scripted or kinematic controllers. Infrastructure-heavy concepts (C13: 50-player grid sim; C18: persistent cross-server entity) are the other hard tier. Most feasible are server-authoritative, low-physics state machines (C06 incremental, C01 anomaly swaps, C02 logic puzzle, C04 inspection UI, C16, C19, C20, C17 with auto-anchoring). Content volume rather than engineering is the main cost for C01 and C04. Any mandatory-N-player design (C02, C12, C15, C20 ranked) needs in-server pads or bots, because cross-server matchmaking at launch CCU is unreliable. Nothing scored 9–10: no concept is trivial at a compelling quality bar.
